business.category: Email API / developer email sending platform

facts.statement: Resend delivers both transactional emails (personalized, event-driven communication) and marketing campaigns (bulk email Broadcasts distributed to a contact list).

facts.statement: Resend started as an open source project in 2022 and launched its full email sending platform in 2023 after joining Y Combinator's winter batch.

Add-on $30 / mo

facts.statement: Data retention is 30 days on Free, Pro, and Scale, and flexible on Enterprise.

provenance.quote: Data retention | 30 days | 30 days | 30 days | Flexible

provenance.quote: const { data, error } = await resend.emails.receiving.list();

facts.statement: Webhooks include automatic retries with exponential backoff and manual replay of failed or successful messages.

provenance.quote: With retries and exponential backoff, you can trust that your critical notifications will maintain the integrity even if there's a temporary system failure. ... Quickly recover from errors by manually replaying failed webhook messages

facts.statement: Automations let customers trigger custom events via API and build multi-step workflows with conditional paths, wait-for-event steps, and time delays.

provenance.quote: Define events with strongly typed schemas and trigger them via API. ... Branch your workflow based on contact data or event properties. ... Pause a workflow until a specific event occurs. ... Add a delay between steps.

facts.statement: Audiences let customers add contacts via API, CSV upload, or manual entry, and Resend automatically handles unsubscribe flows.

provenance.quote: Add custom variables such as first name and last name. Configure a fallback in case these values are undefined. ... Plan the sending day and time of an email broadcast using natural language input such as ”in 1 hour”.

facts.statement: Dynamic email templates let teams collaborate with presence indicators, auto-save, and a full revision history, and be called by template ID and variables when sending.

provenance.quote: Templates enable designers, developers, and marketers to collaborate on templates with presence indicators, auto-save, and a full revision history system. ... include only the template ID and variables in your call.

facts.statement: Resend offers a test mode to simulate events without risking real emails being sent to real people.

provenance.quote: Simulate events and experiment with our API without the risk of accidentally sending real emails to real people.

facts.statement: Resend provides SDKs and integration paths for Node.js, Ruby, Python, PHP, Go, Rust, Java, Elixir, .NET, REST, SMTP, and CLI.

provenance.quote: Node.jsServerlessRubyPythonPHPCLIGoRustJavaElixir.NETRESTSMTP

entries.claim: Supabase custom SMTP is configured under Authentication settings; after saving, Supabase separately imposes a 30-messages-per-hour Auth limit that is adjusted under Authentication > Rate Limits.
entries.verbatim:
Once you've set up your account with an email sending service, head to the [Authentication settings page](/dashboard/project/_/auth/smtp) to enable and configure custom SMTP.

You can also configure custom SMTP using the Management API:

```
1



# Get your access token from https://supabase.com/dashboard/account/tokens



2



export SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN="your-access-token"



3



export PROJECT_REF="your-project-ref"



4



5



# Configure custom SMTP



6



curl -X PATCH "https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/$PROJECT_REF/config/auth" \



7



-H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN" \



8



-H "Content-Type: application/json" \



9



-d '{



10



"external_email_enabled": true,



11



"mailer_secure_email_change_enabled": true,



12



"mailer_autoconfirm": false,



13



"smtp_admin_email": "no-reply@example.com",



14



"smtp_host": "smtp.example.com",



15



"smtp_port": 587,



16



"smtp_user": "your-smtp-user",



17



"smtp_pass": "your-smtp-password",



18



"smtp_sender_name": "Your App Name"



19



}'
```

Once you save these settings, your project's Auth server will send messages to all addresses. To protect the reputation of your newly set up service a low rate-limit of 30 messages per hour is imposed. To adjust this to an acceptable value for your use case head to the [Rate Limits configuration page](/dashboard/project/_/auth/rate-limits).

entries.claim: Resend supplies test recipient addresses for delivered, bounced, and spam-complaint events without affecting domain reputation.
entries.verbatim:
Instead of using your personal email account or setting up a fake SMTP server, you can leverage the following email addresses to simulate each event type.

This gives you full use of Resend's Dashboard, Webhooks, and API - without affecting your domain reputation.

## [Test delivered emails](#test-delivered-emails)

To test that your emails are being successfully delivered, you can send an email to:

```
delivered@resend.dev
```

## [Test bounced emails](#test-bounced-emails)

To test that the recipient's email provider rejected your email, you can send an email to:

```
bounced@resend.dev
```

This will generate an SMTP 550 5.1.1 ("Unknown User") response code.

## [Test "Marked as Spam" emails](#test-marked-as-spam-emails)

To test that your emails are received but marked as spam, you can send an email to:

```
complained@resend.dev
```

voice.tone: Direct and technical, mildly self-assured, allergic to hype and superlatives — problems are named plainly and solutions stated as fact
voice.rhythm: Short declarative sentences, often paired as problem-then-solution; headlines are terse fragments, body copy runs two to three sentences before breaking
exemplars: The web has come a long way in the last ten years, but why is email stuck in the past?
It doesn't have to be that way. We want to change that. We want to reimagine email.
Resend started with an **open source** project in 2022. We were **frustrated** by how difficult it was to build **modern** email templates that **worked well** across all email clients.
We are a team of engineers who love building tools for other engineers. Our goal is to create the email platform we've always wished we had — one that *just works*.
Most providers hand you a cold IP and a warmup spreadsheet. Resend provisions, warms, and maintains it for you.

segments.name: The one backend engineer at a ten-person product team who owns email because nobody else does
segments.situation: Individual engineers integrating a hosted auth platform (Supabase Auth) into a product's signup, password-reset, invite, and OTP flows post first-person accounts, in GitHub issues and discussions on the platform's own repos, of hitting the built-in email rate limit and having to reason through Supabase's dashboard logs, SMTP settings, and plan tiers themselves to diagnose it.

situation_provenance.quote: I am experiencing an issue where authentication emails (magic links/OTP) are blocked with a 429: email rate limit exceeded error, even though I have not exceeded the email limits.
I'm encountering a persistent 429 (Too Many Requests) error with the message AuthApiError: email rate limit exceeded when calling supabase.auth.signUp from my React frontend application.

segments.job_to_be_done: Wants the email rate limit raised to a level they control, via their own SMTP provider and dashboard rate-limit settings, instead of being capped by the built-in provider.
segments.trigger: A 429 email rate limit error firing on sign-up or magic-link/OTP requests, below the documented threshold, prompts the engineer to open a public issue.; The platform's own production-readiness checklist tells engineers to configure their own SMTP for auth emails before launch, and separately flags that a major public announcement will exceed the default rate limit.

pains.statement: Auth email sending (signup confirmation, OTP, magic link, invites) gets blocked with a 429 email rate limit error under normal usage, even when the reporter believes they are under the documented limit.

provenance.quote: The API call fails with 429: email rate limit exceeded, even when sending fewer than 2 emails per hour.

pains.statement: Upgrading the platform's paid subscription tier does not raise the built-in email rate limit; only configuring a separate custom SMTP provider does.

provenance.quote: There is no difference in Pro plan and Free on email rate limit for the built in email provider. You need your own SMTP provider and to set the limit higher in the dashboard rate limit settings under authentication.

pains.statement: An unrelated dashboard action (creating or deleting an Auth Hook) silently wipes the custom SMTP configuration and resets the email rate limit back to a low default, with no warning shown in the UI, and the effect on real auth email only becomes visible later.

provenance.quote: While the Send Email hook is enabled, the wipe is invisible — the hook bypasses SMTP entirely, so mail keeps flowing. The failure only surfaces later, when the hook is disabled for any reason, at which point ALL auth email stops silently and completely.

pains.statement: It is unclear to the reporter how the platform counts emails and API calls toward its documented rate limit, since the observed failure point does not match the documented threshold.

provenance.quote: How does Supabase count the number of emails sent for signup auth confirmation, as it's shown that 30 is rate limit per hour but rate limit exceed after 3-4 signup confirmation been sent, please help?

pains.statement: Mixing transactional and marketing email sending on the same provider/domain creates a deliverability risk: a marketing-driven spam complaint or unsubscribe spike can get the account suspended and take down transactional (auth-critical) sending with it.

provenance.quote: One advice I've seen is not to mix transactional and marketing providers (and ideally domains). If you get a high incidence of unsubscribes or "this is spam" responses, don't want your app to be dead in the water for transactional stuff if the marketing provider suspends your account temporarily (can happen even if you're legit).

pains.statement: A homegrown transactional-email setup (enums, templates, tracking) that starts simple for signup/password-reset grows into an unwieldy system as a SaaS product and its users grow, without anyone wanting to fully outsource it.

provenance.quote: Every SaaS app will start off with some code to send email for the basic functions of signup, password reset, maybe eventually billing, inviting new users to the account.

segments.name: The one backend engineer at a 20-person dev-tools company who owns email because nobody else does
segments.situation: Their week is features, reviews and on-call. Email is not their job but it is their responsibility: password resets, magic links, team invites, receipts and alerts all leave through a provider someone wired up two years ago, or through an SMTP wrapper they inherited. Templates are likely HTML strings in the repo, edited by whoever last touched them, and testing one means sending it to yourself. They typically only look at the sending layer when it fails — a support ticket says a reset link never arrived and they go hunting for a single message ID in a dashboard that was designed for a marketing team. Named customers in this shape describe the same posture in their own words: a small team that does not want to think about email infrastructure at all, engineers who would rather build features than troubleshoot it, and an infra CTO who rates debugging as the thing that matters. Nobody in the company owns deliverability; the DNS records were set once and never looked at again.

segments.name: The engineer at a growing product whose users keep saying "I never got the email"
segments.situation: Their product's core loop runs on mail that must arrive: security alerts, invites, receipts, verification codes. Volume has climbed past the point where one bad week is invisible — plausibly past the thousands-per-day mark where providers start talking about dedicated IPs. Support answers 'check your spam folder' more often than anyone is comfortable with, and each instance is unfalsifiable from the inside: the provider says delivered, the customer says nothing arrived. SPF and DKIM were set up at some point; DMARC may or may not exist. They are sharing an IP pool with senders they cannot see or control, and the standard advice — get a dedicated IP — comes with a warmup schedule they have no time or expertise to run, and a known failure mode where a botched ramp makes deliverability worse than the pool they left. At least one named Resend customer, Infisical, describes exactly this before-state: complaints about emails landing in spam that stopped after switching to dedicated IPs.

provenance.quote: Most providers hand you a cold IP and a warmup spreadsheet. Resend provisions, warms, and maintains it for you.

pains.statement: Likely: their traffic is uneven — product launches, batch notifications, quiet weekends — which is precisely the profile where a dedicated IP can hurt rather than help, so the recommended fix is not obviously safe for them.
Likely: they cannot prove the problem internally. Without per-recipient event data they have anecdotes from support and no way to show leadership whether deliverability is degrading or steady.
Likely: reputation feels out of their hands on a shared pool, because the neighbours on that IP are invisible to them and their own good behaviour does not insulate them.

segments.name: The technical founder who also sends the product newsletter, and whose welcome sequence is a cron job
segments.situation: Transactional mail is solved enough to ignore; the lifecycle side is not. New-user onboarding emails are hand-built — a table recording who received which message, a scheduled job, a few conditionals — so adding a step or changing a delay means a deploy and a migration, and a bug means somebody gets day three twice. The contact list for product updates likely lives in a separate marketing tool, populated by CSV export, which means two systems, two senders and two places an unsubscribe has to be honoured. When a designer or a first marketing hire arrives, they cannot touch any of it without a pull request. Jellypod's founder describes the before-state of the workflow half of this directly — a hand-built, tangled setup for multi-day welcome sequences — and Hike Medical's co-founder describes what he actually wants from the list half: reporting he can trust and an interface that gets out of the way so the team can communicate with users.

segments.job_to_be_done: Have new users get the right message at the right moment without maintaining a second codebase to make it happen — and be able to send an update to everyone without it becoming an engineering ticket.
segments.trigger: An activation or onboarding push where the sequence needs to change weekly and the hand-rolled version cannot keep up; or the first marketing or design hire who needs to edit an email and cannot; or the marketing tool's bill stepping up as the contact list grows; or launching a second brand or customer-facing domain.

pains.statement: Resend asserts that unsubscribe handling is work the sender otherwise carries — it claims to run the flow and skip unsubscribed contacts on the next Broadcast. Vendor framing of the burden.

provenance.quote: When a contact unsubscribes, Resend will automatically handle the unsubscribe flow for you, and they will be skipped when sending the next Broadcast.

pains.statement: Likely: transactional mail and marketing mail sit in different systems, so there are two sending reputations to maintain, two sets of logs to search and two places a suppression has to be honoured.
Likely: changing the timing or copy of a lifecycle email requires an engineer and a deploy, so experiments that should take an afternoon take a sprint.
Likely: nobody is confident the sequence is actually firing correctly for every user, because the only record of who got what is a table they wrote themselves.

objections.objection: We already have a provider wired into sign-up and billing; re-doing DNS and touching those code paths is risk with no visible upside
We already have SendGrid/SES/Postmark and it mostly works. Migrating the thing that sends password resets is a multi-week project with real blast radius, and nobody wants to own it.
objections.answer: The strongest counter in the evidence is that the first step is small, not that the migration is small. Raycast moved from SendGrid and got their first real test — waitlist emails for the iOS and Windows apps — done inside 30 minutes [E337, E338, E320]. Braintrust's engineer says taking it into production had no friction at all [E323]. The entry path is deliberately low-commitment: 9-12 official SDKs plus plain REST and an SMTP relay, so an SMTP-only swap needs no application code [E301, E236, E237], and test mode lets the cutover be rehearsed without any risk of real email reaching real people [E300]. What the evidence does not answer: nothing covers migrating suppression lists, historical logs or IP reputation, and data retention is 30 days on every plan below Enterprise [E251], so history does not come along.

objections.objection: I cannot tell what this costs. Plan prices are not in front of me, and I am not opening a migration on an unknown monthly bill that scales with volume.
objections.answer: Partially answerable, and the gap must be stated rather than papered over. The units that are published: Free is 3,000 emails/mo capped at 100/day [E284, E233], Pro includes 50,000/mo [E286], Scale includes 100,000/mo [E289], overage is $0.90 per 1,000 emails on Pro and Scale [E287, E299], automations are 10,000 runs free then $0.0015/run [E298, E297], and the add-ons are explicitly priced — domains $20/mo, dedicated IPs $30/mo, SSO $150/mo [E225, E228, E231]. The monthly price of Pro and Scale is not in the evidence at all, so no email can quote a headline figure or claim a saving against the incumbent; the honest move is to send them to the pricing page rather than invent a number.

objections.objection: Deliverability is the only reason I would move, and no provider can actually promise my mail reaches inboxes. Switching usually means a reputation dip before it gets better.
objections.answer: Weakly answered, and this is the most important gap in the whole evidence base. There is exactly one named customer outcome: Infisical's co-founder says complaints about spam stopped after moving to dedicated IPs [E13, E326, E327]. One testimonial is one customer's experience, not a rate. Everything else is mechanism rather than result: automatic warmup with no waiting period [E16, E309], round-the-clock reputation monitoring that flags issues before they hit the inbox [E17], an autoscaling IP pool [E18], pristine shared IPs [E247], DNSBL/Spamhaus monitoring with removal requests generated automatically [E306], DNS configuration monitoring [E311], DKIM/SPF/DMARC support [E253, E312, E314], an automatic suppression list [E310, E248], and BIMI guidance [E308]. There is no inbox-placement rate, no benchmark and no before/after figure anywhere in the evidence. Deliverability expertise is also not included on Free [E269], so the person evaluating cheaply gets none of the human help.

objections.objection: I could build this on SES for a fraction of the cost. It is an API call and a queue.
objections.answer: Partially answered. The evidence contains one customer who did build it and moved off: Jellypod's founder calls their hand-built lifecycle setup tangled before replacing it [E27]. The parts nobody wants to maintain and that are on the shelf here: webhook retries with exponential backoff plus manual replay of failed or successful messages [E53, E54], automatic unsubscribe handling and suppression [E52, E310, E248], managed IP provisioning, warmup and autoscaling rather than a warmup spreadsheet [E15, E16, E230], React Email as a component library instead of hand-written HTML [E303], collaborative templates with auto-save and full revision history callable by ID and variables [E45, E46, E47], and inbound parsing with attachments delivered as structured data [E57, E60]. What is missing: no cost comparison against self-hosting exists in the evidence, so the build-vs-buy argument can only be made on maintenance, never on price.

objections.objection: Our marketing team will not give up Mailchimp/Customer.io for this. Where is A/B testing, segmentation, and more than a month of reporting history?
objections.answer: Partially answered, and parity must not be claimed. What exists: Broadcasts with a WYSIWYG editor and Markdown, personalization variables with fallbacks, natural-language scheduling, and open/click tracking showing who opened and which links each person clicked [E33, E34, E35, E36]; Automations with conditional paths on contact data or event properties, wait-for-event steps and delays from minutes to weeks [E25, E23, E24]; Audiences populated by API, CSV with field mapping, or manual entry, with unsubscribes handled automatically [E49, E48, E52]; and one marketing-side customer voice [E50, E51]. What is absent from the evidence entirely: A/B testing, list segmentation as a feature, and any reporting beyond the 30-day data retention that applies to Free, Pro and Scale alike [E251]. For a team that reports on cohorts quarter over quarter, that retention limit is a genuine blocker and should be conceded, not dodged.

objections.objection: We are not routing customer data through a company that launched in 2023. Security review will ask for SOC 2, SSO and an uptime SLA before I can even trial it.
objections.answer: Mostly answered, with real gaps worth naming first. Included on every plan, Free upward: SOC 2 Type II certification, GDPR compliance, penetration testing, DDoS protection, automated backups, multi-factor authentication, API key permissions and signed webhook endpoints [E259, E258, E260, E261, E262, E263, E264, E265]. Company standing: platform launched in 2023 out of Y Combinator's winter batch, $18M Series A, three named founders [E7, E8, E9, E10]. Named customers a reviewer will recognise: eBay, Warner Bros, Decathlon, Supabase, Mistral AI, Chicago Blackhawks, Beast Industries [E77, E71, E199, E194, E208, E214, E74]. The gaps: Single Sign-On is a $150/mo add-on and only from Scale up, included only on Enterprise [E231, E232, E257]; the 99.99% uptime SLA is Enterprise-only [E291]; an urgent response SLA starts at Scale [E268]; and 30-day data retention below Enterprise [E251] will fail some audit requirements outright.

objections.objection: Nothing is on fire. Email works well enough this quarter, and this is not what I am being measured on.
objections.answer: Not answered by the evidence, and that should be said plainly downstream: there is no urgency argument available, no deadline, no deprecation, no price change, no documented cost of waiting. The only lever is making the evaluation smaller than the objection — Raycast's first real test took 30 minutes [E337], the free entry needs no credit card [E31], the Free plan carries the real API, SMTP relay, official SDKs and React Email rather than a crippled trial [E235, E236, E237, E242], and test mode means the experiment cannot touch a real recipient [E300]. The counter-pressure to acknowledge: Free is capped at 100 emails a day [E233], so a genuine volume test cannot happen without a paid plan.

objections.objection: I am the one who wants to send the emails and I am not an engineer. Getting started apparently needs a verified domain and an API key, which means I am blocked on someone else.
objections.answer: Honestly only half-answered. Setup genuinely requires a verified domain and a Resend API key, which is an engineer's task, and nothing in the evidence describes a marketer-only onboarding path. After setup the day-to-day is not developer-gated: Templates is explicitly built for designers, developers and marketers to work in together with presence indicators, auto-save, revision history and a publish flow [E45, E46]; Broadcasts is a WYSIWYG editor with Markdown, variables with fallbacks and natural-language scheduling [E34, E35, E33]; contacts import from a CSV with field mapping or by manual entry [E48]; and Hike Medical's co-founder singles out the clean interface and accurate reporting [E50]. The copy should concede the one-time engineering dependency rather than imply self-serve setup.

objections.objection: Everyone tells me a dedicated IP fixes spam. If I pay $30/mo for one and my volume is spiky, am I just buying a worse reputation and an upsell?
objections.answer: Well answered, and unusually in the buyer's favour. Resend's own dedicated IP page argues against selling it to most readers: mailbox providers weigh domain reputation more than the IP, a dedicated IP only pays off for high-volume consistent senders, and a well-monitored shared IP delivers better from day one for small, spiky or still-building senders. The add-on is gated accordingly — Scale and up, for senders exceeding 3,000 emails per day [E20, E229, E245] at $30/mo [E19, E228] — and there is a published guide on whether you need one at all. For those who do qualify, warmup, monitoring and autoscaling are run by Resend rather than handed over as a spreadsheet [E15, E16, E17, E18, E230], and IP warming is included at Scale [E246]. No buyer in the evidence is recorded raising this objection; it is inferred from the fact that Resend devotes a page and a blog post to answering it.

provenance.quote: Available on the Scale plan and up, for senders sending more than 3,000 emails per day.
